To use the `wpa_passphrase`–encrypted PSK, you can either copy and paste the encrypted PSK into the `wpa_supplicant.conf` file, or redirect the tools output to the configuration file in one of two ways:
- Either change to `root` by executing `sudo su`, then call `wpa_passphrase "testing" >> /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf` and enter the password when asked
- Or use `wpa_passphrase "testing" | sudo tee -a /etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant.conf > /dev/null` and give it the testing password when asked; the redirection to `/dev/null` prevents `tee` from **also** outputting to the screen (standard output)

If you want to use one of these two options, **make sure you use `>>`, or use `-a` with `tee`** — either will **append** text to an existing file. Using a single chevron `>`, or omitting `-a` when using `tee`, will erase all contents and **then** append the output to the specified file.

Routers route or drop traffic whether they have a relevant route for it, or not. Firewalls filter traffic that isn't dropped.
Between a source and a destination host (and back again), each router along the path makes a _fatal_ decision (pass/drop) based on the _local information_ it has.

Say a wifi client 192.168.4.99 queries Google's DNS 8.8.8.8, and receives a response; The path includes 2 local routers:  Pi > ISP router > (internet routers) > ISP router > Pi. Any router can break the chain.
Internet routers automatically exchange routes, they know their stuff. Local routers require local administration...
 - The Pi router knows all networks involved, it will let traffic pass. 
 - The ISP router does not know about network 192.168.4.0/24, it _will_ drop traffic (on they way out sometimes, on the way in always).
The simplest and most portable solution is to hide the hosts in this network under the identity of the Pi, using the well-known LAN address 10.10.0.2.

Tutorials all choose this double-NAT solution. None (I think) try to explain the reason for  masquerading. So let me try again:

Enabling routing will allow hosts from network `192.168.4.0/24` to reach the LAN and the main router towards the internet. 
In order to ensure that, in turn, the main router will allow traffic between wireless clients and the internet, the Raspberry Pi can substitute their IP address with its own IP address on the LAN using a "masquerade" firewall rule.

Hope that's more clear.

Yes to both suggestions.

Yes, 432MHz is incorrect (it may have been correct before DVFS firmware changes some months ago). core_freq is largely ignored.

PLLC is set based on hdmi_enable_4kp60/enable_tvout. Currently that is:
3000 default
3300 hdmi_enable_4kp60
3240 enable_tvout

There is then a fixed divide by 3 for the channel frequency:
1000 default
1100 hdmi_enable_4kp60
1080 enable_tvout

We then pick the integer divider that doesn't exceed core_freq where:
core_freq=550 hdmi_enable_4kp60
core_freq=500 otherwise

You can specify other core_freq values that are integer divisors of the channel frequency.
There are very few options that work. core_freq=1000 will never boot. Any others are underclocks (which are supported - e.g. core_freq=333 for default display case).
Technically enable_tvout=1 core_freq=540 (with a suitable over_voltage) should be possible but that is a very niche case.

But these are all implementation details that will likely change during the lifetime of Pi4 and as such I don't think they are worth documenting in detail. Currently there is almost nothing that can usefully be done by a user to overclock core freq. But that could change.

Something roughly like:
```
Pi4 powers on
BCM2711 looks for recovery.bin on first partition of SD card
if recovery.bin exists (and is "a valid executable"):
    BCM2711 loads and runs recovery.bin
    recovery.bin looks for pieeprom.upd on first partition of SD card
    if pieeprom.upd exists:
        recovery.bin flashes pieeprom.upd to EEPROM
        recovery.bin renames itself to recovery.000
        recovery.bin resets the BCM2711, go back to start
    else:
        recovery.bin looks for pieeprom.bin on first partition of SD card
        if pieeprom.bin exists:
            recovery.bin flashes pieeprom.bin to EEPROM
            recovery.bin halts the BCM2711
else:
    BCM2711 loads and runs the bootloader from EEPROM
    bootloader reads the bootloader config from EEPROM
    bootloader does whatever BOOT_ORDER requires it to do
    bootloader reads config.txt either from SD card, USB HDD or TFTP, according to previous step
    if bootloader[FREEZE_VERSION] == 0:
        if bootloader[ENABLE_SELF_UPDATE] == 1 and config.txt[bootloader_update] == 1:
            bootloader looks for pieeprom.upd (either from SD card, USB HDD or TFTP, according to the BOOT_ORDER step)
            if pieeprom.upd exists:
                bootloader reads version of pieeprom.upd
                if version of pieeprom.upd != version of running bootloader:
                    bootloader flashes pieeprom.upd to EEPROM
                    bootloader resets the BCM2711, go back to start
    bootloader loads and runs start4.elf (either from SD card, USB HDD or TFTP, according to the BOOT_ORDER step)
    start4.elf loads and runs the Linux kernel (either from SD card, USB HDD or TFTP, according to the BOOT_ORDER step), passing it options from cmdline.txt
    Linux kernel mounts its root filesystem according to cmdline options
```
(for brevity, I've omitted details about the vl805 firmware and the bootloader signature files)

And then `rpi-eeprom-update` (run from within Linux) works by copying (when FREEZE_VERSION==0) `pieeprom.upd` and `recovery.bin` to the Linux boot partition. (I guess _theoretically_, `rpi-eeprom-update` only needs to copy `recovery.bin` to the boot partition if it's booted from SD card and ENABLE_SELF_UPDATE==0, but the file is less than 100KB so it doesn't hurt to always copy it)

And the linux [systemd service](https://github.com/raspberrypi/rpi-eeprom/blob/debian/buster/debian/rpi-eeprom.rpi-eeprom-update.service) just runs `rpi-eeprom-update -a` once during each time the Pi boots up.

And the "recovery images" on https://www.raspberrypi.org/downloads/ work by writing `pieeprom.bin` and `recovery.bin` to a blank SD card.
